--- title: "Template: Why I Chose This Method" subtitle: "A reusable structure for project write-ups, shown with a small A/B test example." date: 2026-11-01 categories: [template, experimentation, statistics] image: thumbnail.png draft: true jupyter: python3 --- ## TL;DR > One or two sentences: the question, the answer, and the decision it supports. > > *Example:* A new checkout button increased conversion by about 1.3 percentage points > (95% CI roughly 0.1–2.5 pp), so I'd recommend rolling it out, while monitoring refund rates. ## 1. The question What decision is this analysis supposed to inform? Who would act on it? *Example:* A (simulated) online store tested a redesigned checkout button. The product team wants to know: **should we ship it?** ## 2. The data Where it came from, how much there is, and anything suspicious about it. ::: {#cell-setup .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Simulate the experiment data"} import numpy as np import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt rng = np.random.default_rng(42) n_per_group = 5000 true_rates = {"control": 0.100, "treatment": 0.113} df = pd.DataFrame({ "group": np.repeat(list(true_rates), n_per_group), }) df["converted"] = rng.random(len(df)) < df["group"].map(true_rates) summary = df.groupby("group")["converted"].agg(users="size", conversions="sum", rate="mean") summary.style.format({"rate": "{:.2%}"}) ``` ::: {#setup .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}
  users conversions rate
group      
control 5000 492 9.84%
treatment 5000 559 11.18%
``` ::: ::: ## 3. Options I considered | Option | Pros | Cons | |---|---|---| | Two-proportion z-test | Fast, standard, easy to explain | Relies on a normal approximation | | **Bootstrap confidence interval** | Few assumptions; gives an interval for the lift directly | Slower; results vary slightly by seed | | Bayesian A/B test | "Probability treatment is better" is intuitive | Needs a prior; harder to explain to some audiences | ## 4. What I chose, and why I chose the **bootstrap**, because the audience cares about *how big* the lift is, not only whether it is "significant", and the bootstrap produces an interval for the lift without extra assumptions. I still ran the z-test as a sanity check. ::: {#bootstrap .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} c = df.loc[df.group == "control", "converted"].to_numpy() t = df.loc[df.group == "treatment", "converted"].to_numpy() n_boot = 5000 lifts = np.array([ rng.choice(t, t.size).mean() - rng.choice(c, c.size).mean() for _ in range(n_boot) ]) observed = t.mean() - c.mean() low, high = np.percentile(lifts, [2.5, 97.5]) print(f"Observed lift: {observed:+.2%} (95% CI: {low:+.2%} to {high:+.2%})") # Sanity check: two-proportion z-test from math import erf, sqrt p_pool = (t.sum() + c.sum()) / (t.size + c.size) se = sqrt(p_pool * (1 - p_pool) * (1 / t.size + 1 / c.size)) z = observed / se p_value = 2 * (1 - 0.5 * (1 + erf(abs(z) / sqrt(2)))) print(f"z-test: z = {z:.2f}, p = {p_value:.3f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Observed lift: +1.34% (95% CI: +0.14% to +2.54%) z-test: z = 2.18, p = 0.029 ``` ::: ::: ## 5. Results ::: {#cell-fig-lift .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.5)) ax.hist(lifts * 100, bins=50, color="#2780e3", alpha=0.8) ax.axvspan(low * 100, high * 100, color="#2780e3", alpha=0.12) ax.axvline(0, color="gray", linestyle="--", linewidth=1) ax.set_xlabel("Lift in conversion rate (percentage points)") ax.set_ylabel("Bootstrap samples") ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False) plt.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Bootstrap distribution of the conversion lift. The shaded band is the 95% interval.](index_files/figure-html/fig-lift-output-1.png){#fig-lift width=662 height=326} ::: ::: The interval does not include zero, and the z-test agrees. ## 6. Trade-offs and limitations What did I give up by choosing this method? What could make the result wrong? - The bootstrap gives slightly different numbers with a different seed. - The test only measured *conversion*. A button that converts more could also increase refunds. - Two weeks of data may include a novelty effect. ## 7. So what? ::: {.callout-tip} ## Recommendation Ship the new button, and track refund rate for the next month. If I had more time, I would check whether the lift differs between new and returning users. ::: ## 8. What I'd do differently Honest reflection. *Example:* I would decide the sample size *before* running the test (power analysis) instead of after. --- *Code for this post: [GitHub link](https://github.com/jhwn223)*
